content.page_summary: Guidance on management of patients with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis and management of low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis (see Figure 16). Discusses indications for aortic valve intervention (TAVI vs SAVR), patient selection by age and surgical risk, the role of the Heart Team, and prerequisites (exclude other causes of high flow).
key_recommendations: In patients with suspected symptomatic and severe high-gradient aortic stenosis (valve area ≤1 cm², mean gradient ≥40 mmHg), exclude and correct other causes of high-flow status (e.g., anaemia, hyperthyroidism, arteriovenous shunts) before valve intervention.
An aortic valve intervention is recommended in patients with heart failure (HF) symptoms and severe, high-gradient aortic stenosis, regardless of LVEF.
Intervention is recommended in patients with life expectancy > 1 year and when not futile.
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is non-inferior to surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) for reducing clinical events in patients at high and intermediate surgical risk.
For low surgical risk and patients aged <75 years, SAVR is recommended (STS-PROM or EuroSCORE II <4%).
TAVI is recommended for patients aged >75 years or at high/prohibitive surgical risk (STS-PROM or EuroSCORE II >8%).
In other cases, decision between TAVI and SAVR should be individualized by the Heart Team, weighing age, life expectancy, patient preference, clinical and anatomical features.
Aortic valve interventions should be performed in centers with both interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery services and a structured collaborative Heart Team.
content.low_flow_low_gradient_management_summary: Refer to Figure 16. For suspected severe low-flow low-gradient AS with heart failure: assess LVEF and perform dobutamine stress echocardiography if LVEF <50%. Evaluate flow reserve. If diagnostic uncertainty, assess aortic valve calcium score by CT. High calcium score supports severe AS and referral to Heart Team for consideration of SAVR or TAVI. If not severe by criteria or low calcium score, follow-up and conservative management may be appropriate. Medical therapy optimization is recommended when indicated.

figure_16_notes_and_thresholds.figure_title: Management of patients with severe low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis and heart failure
key_thresholds_and_definitions: Age >70 years noted as a contextual consideration
diagnostic_steps_in_flowchart: If LVEF <50% → consider dobutamine echocardiography to assess flow reserve.
Assess flow reserve result: presence/absence guides diagnosis of severe low-flow low-gradient AS.
If no flow reserve or inconclusive, use CT aortic valve calcium score to help determine severity.
High calcium score → Heart Team evaluation → consider SAVR (Class I/IIa) or TAVI (Class I/IIa) depending on risk/age.
If criteria not met → follow-up and medical therapy optimization.

abbreviations_from_caption.EuroSCORE II: European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II
abbreviations_from_caption.STS-PROM: Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality

patient_selection_points: Avoid futile interventions; consider life expectancy (>1 year) and comorbidities.
Consider patient age, surgical risk scores (STS-PROM, EuroSCORE II), individual preference and anatomical features when selecting TAVI vs SAVR.
Heart Team should weigh pros and cons of each procedure for each patient.
content.operational_recommendation: Valve interventions should be performed in centers with both interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery services on site and a structured collaborative Heart Team approach.
